Subject: Discovery Recap: latency & concurrency targets (Finly)

Hi Alex / Priya —

Thanks again for taking the time today. Quick recap from our call and the action items we agreed on. Please reply if I missed anything.

Summary of pain / goals
- Primary pain: production latency spikes during peak trading windows causing poor UX for real-time recommendations.
- Goal: consistent p95 generation latency and a smooth streaming UX for multi-turn interactions in the trading console.
- Success criteria (what you told us):
  - Non-streaming p95 <= 300ms for average prompt size (~250 tokens) under expected steady-state load.
  - Streaming first-byte p95 <= 400ms and steady-stream p95 <= 600ms for long responses (up to ~2k tokens) so users see token streaming without stutter.
  - Sustained concurrency target: 200-300 concurrent live streaming sessions during high-volume windows; burst to 500 for short windows.

Current stack / constraints
- You currently run an in-house microservice layered on a hosted LLM provider for generation; also maintain a local caching layer for common prompts.
- Hard requirement: data residency in us-east and strict audit trail for inference logs (SOC2 compliance ongoing).

Immediate next steps / ask from Redwood
1) We (Redwood) will run a scoped perf PoC: benchmark your representative prompts against our hosted/dedicated configs to validate p95 targets at your concurrency profile.
2) You’ll share: a) a representative prompt set and average token lengths, b) a sample anonymized traffic replay (or ask us for a small runner).
3) We'll deliver: capacity estimate, cost forecast, and recommended rollout (dedicated vs hosted + fallback policy).

Timeline
- PoC kickoff: week of 5/24 (subject to your availability).
- Initial perf report: ~1 week after kickoff.

Attachments: none in this mail — Aditya will follow up with a quick capacity estimate and baseline notes.

Thanks — talk soon.
— Marissa

Marissa — thanks for the summary, this looks accurate. A couple clarifications from our side:

1) The 200-300 concurrent sessions figure is for our web UI (trading ops). Separate batch scoring runs happen off-hours and are lower priority for the PoC.
2) For streaming UX, the most important metric is time-to-first-token for user perception; the steady-state streaming p95 target is relaxed but we do care about smoothness (no >200ms gaps between tokens).

We can share a sample prompt set and a replay extract — I'll follow up with Priya to drop that into the shared Drive. Also curious on cost delta between a dedicated pool sized for 300 concurrent streams vs a hosted-burst strategy.

Alex / Marissa — adding a few technical notes from our side and attaching a quick capacity estimate and the baseline jperf results we ran against a small cluster (see attachments).

Technical notes
- The p95 numbers need to be validated against your prompt complexity and tokenization. We typically benchmark with "short" (~150 tokens), "medium" (~500 tokens), and "long" (~2k tokens) buckets. Your 250-token average fits in our "short/medium" buckets.
- Streaming performance is heavily influenced by model selection (decoder-only vs chat optimized), batching behavior, and prefix caching. For smooth streaming at 300 concurrent sessions, Dedicated GPU pools with optimized KV cache hit rates are usually the most predictable.
- Fallback policy: we recommend a warm standby of a smaller model or lower-quality quantized model for short bursts to avoid dropped requests.

Attachments:
- initial_capacity_estimate.xlsx (high-level nodes / GPU types / cost)
- baseline-jperf-results.txt (raw perf logs)

Next steps (technical)
- If you can share a 10-20 prompt sample and a short traffic replay (1-2 minutes), we can create an airflow job to replay on our test harness and validate p95 targets under simulated concurrency.
- We'll also prepare a model/config recommendation matrix for streaming vs non-streaming endpoints.

— Aditya
